blocks.h: 1. The Code, and what made it mandatory

blocks.p: The IMO Instruments Implementation Code (III Code) is the annex to resolution A.1070(28), adopted by the Assembly on 4 December 2013. It revoked resolution A.1054(27), the Code for the Implementation of Mandatory IMO Instruments, 2011 (operative paragraph 3), which had been the basis of the voluntary audit scheme.

The Code is recommendatory in its own drafting - it says what a State "should" do - but its use was made mandatory by amendments to the treaty instruments themselves: A.1083(28), A.1084(28) and A.1085(28) amended Load Lines 1966, Tonnage 1969 and COLREG 1972; MSC.366(93), MSC.373(93), MSC.374(93) and MSC.375(93) amended SOLAS 1974, STCW 1978, the STCW Code and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; and MEPC.246(66) and MEPC.247(66) amended MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol. That chain is what turns the Code into the standard against which a Member State is audited under the IMO Member State Audit Scheme.

The Code has four parts: Part 1 Common Areas, Part 2 Flag States, Part 3 Coastal States and Part 4 Port States. Each of Parts 2, 3 and 4 ends with an Evaluation and review section, which is where limb (b) lives.

Paragraph 1 states the objective in one sentence: to enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment, and to assist States in the implementation of instruments of the Organization. The second half matters as much as the first - the Code is an assistance instrument, written because the Organization accepted that some States face real difficulty in complying fully.

Paragraph 2 qualifies it. Different States will view the Code according to their own circumstances and should be bound only for the implementation of those instruments to which they are Contracting Governments or Parties; by virtue of geography and circumstance some States have a greater role as a flag State, others as a coastal or port State. The Code is therefore not a uniform checklist applied identically everywhere.

Two general provisions frame everything that follows. Paragraph 4 makes States responsible for promulgating laws and regulations and taking all other steps necessary to give those instruments full and complete effect. Paragraph 5 requires that, in acting against pollution, States must not transfer damage or hazards from one area to another, nor transform one type of pollution into another.

blocks.h: 3. The strategy recommended to the flag State

blocks.p: Paragraph 3 is the answer to the second half of limb (a). To meet the objective, a State is recommended to:

ul: develop an overall strategy to ensure that its international obligations and responsibilities as a flag, port and coastal State are met (3.1);
establish a methodology to monitor and assess that the strategy ensures effective implementation and enforcement of relevant international mandatory instruments (3.2); and
continuously review the strategy to achieve, maintain and improve overall organizational performance and capability as a flag, port and coastal State (3.3).

blocks.p: Read together those three are a develop - monitor - review cycle, not a document to be written once. Paragraph 9 completes it: the State should communicate its strategy, including information on its national legislation, to all concerned.

Paragraph 7 tells the State what its legislation and administrative procedures must actually address - nine areas: jurisdiction; organization and authority; legislation, rules and regulations; promulgation of the applicable mandatory instruments; enforcement arrangements; control, survey, inspection, audit, verification, approval and certification functions; the selection, recognition, authorization, empowerment and monitoring of recognized organizations and nominated surveyors; investigations required to be reported to the Organization; and reporting to the Organization and other Administrations. Paragraph 8 adds the three initial actions a Government must be capable of when a new or amended instrument enters into force: the ability to promulgate laws giving effective jurisdiction and control, a legal basis for enforcement including investigative and penal processes, and sufficient personnel with maritime expertise.

blocks.h: 4. Which IMO instruments the Code covers

blocks.p: This limb has two correct answers and they are not the same, which is where marks are usually lost.
First, the Code's own scope. Paragraph 6 says the Code addresses those aspects necessary to give full and complete effect to the applicable international instruments pertaining to six subject areas:

ul: safety of life at sea;
prevention of pollution from ships;
standards of training, certification and watchkeeping for seafarers;
load lines;
tonnage measurement of ships; and
regulations for preventing collisions at sea.

blocks.p: Note what is absent: maritime security is not one of the six. The preamble to the resolution speaks of safety, security and protection of the marine environment, but the operative scope at paragraph 6 does not extend to the ISPS Code or SOLAS chapter XI-2.

Second, the treaty instruments under which use of the Code is mandatory, and which therefore define the audit scope. These are the instruments listed in resolution A.1187(33) (6 December 2023), the 2023 Non-exhaustive list of obligations under instruments relevant to the III Code: SOLAS 1974 with its 1978 and 1988 Protocols; MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol; STCW 1978 and the STCW Code; Load Lines 1966 and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; Tonnage 1969; and COLREG 1972. A.1187(33) revoked the 2021 list, A.1157(32), so it is the current list at this sitting; its annexes divide the obligations into those of Contracting Governments generally and those specific to flag, coastal and port States.

blocks.h: 5. Key performance indicators for flag State evaluation

blocks.p: Paragraph 42 requires a flag State to evaluate its performance on a periodic basis with respect to the administrative processes, procedures and resources needed to meet its obligations. Paragraph 43 then lists the measures, inter alia:

ul: port State control detention rates;
flag State inspection results;
casualty statistics;
communication and information processes;
annual loss statistics, excluding constructive total losses (CTLs); and
such other performance indicators as may be appropriate.

blocks.p: The stated purpose is diagnostic, and quoting it earns the mark: the indicators exist in order to determine whether staffing, resources and administrative procedures are adequate to meet its flag State obligations.

Paragraph 44 then recommends ten areas for regular review: fleet loss and accident ratios, to identify trends over selected time periods; the number of verified cases of detained ships in relation to the size of the fleet; verified cases of incompetence or wrongdoing by holders of certificates or endorsements issued under its authority; responses to port State deficiency reports or interventions; investigations into very serious and serious casualties and the lessons learned; technical and other resources committed; results of inspections, surveys and controls of ships in the fleet; investigation of occupational accidents; the number of incidents and violations under the applicable international pollution prevention regulations; and the number of suspensions or withdrawals of certificates, endorsements or approvals.
Part 2 is the longest part of the Code, paragraphs 15 to 44. Its structure is implementation - delegation - enforcement - surveyors - investigations - review.

ul: Implementation (15-17). Issue national legislation and guidance implementing the safety and pollution conventions, and assign responsibility for keeping it updated. Paragraph 16 requires a safety and environmental protection programme with five minimum elements, of which the load-bearing one is 16.2: compliance verified by an audit and inspection programme independent of any body issuing the certificates. Paragraph 17 requires ships to be sufficiently and efficiently manned, on the Principles of Safe Manning.

Delegation of authority (18-21). A flag State authorising a recognized organization must determine that it has adequate technical, managerial and research capability; base the authorisation on a formal written agreement; issue specific instructions for a ship found unfit to proceed to sea; supply its national law and interpretations; and require the organization to keep records. Paragraph 20 requires an oversight programme with supplementary surveys and competent supervising staff.

Enforcement (22-27). Prohibit a ship from sailing until it complies; inspect periodically to verify that the actual condition of ship and crew matches the certificates; verify seafarer familiarity and the complement's ability to coordinate in an emergency; provide penalties of adequate severity for ships and for certificate holders; and institute proceedings after investigation irrespective of where the violation occurred. Paragraphs 26 and 27 permit certification only after determining that all applicable requirements are met.

Surveyors and investigations (28-41). Surveyors must be qualified against a defined standard, worked under a documented qualification system, and issued an identification document. Marine safety investigations must be by impartial and objective investigators; casualties are investigated taking account of the Casualty Investigation Code and the report is forwarded to the Organization with the flag State's observations.

blocks.h: 7. Coastal State and port State responsibilities

blocks.p: Parts 3 and 4 open with the same principle, at paragraphs 45 and 52: coastal and port States have rights as well as obligations, and when they exercise those rights they incur additional obligations. Both must implement policy through national legislation and guidance (46, 54) and ensure their legislation and procedures deliver consistent implementation and verification (47, 55).

Coastal State (Part 3). Paragraph 48 lists the rights, obligations and responsibilities, inter alia: radiocommunication services; meteorological services and warnings; search and rescue services; hydrographic services; ships' routeing; ship reporting systems; vessel traffic services; and aids to navigation - eight service areas, and note that they are services to shipping, not controls over ships. Paragraph 50 requires a control and monitoring programme to allocate statistical data for trend analysis, to establish mechanisms for timely response to pollution incidents in its waters, and to cooperate with flag and port States in casualty investigations.

Port State (Part 4). Paragraph 53 records that the port State role derives from a combination of treaties, conventions, national laws and in some cases bilateral and multilateral agreements. Paragraph 56 gives three obligations: provision of appropriate reception facilities or capability to accept all waste streams regulated under IMO instruments; port State control; and keeping a register of fuel oil suppliers. Paragraph 59 carries the no more favourable treatment principle - the port State must impose the conditions of those instruments on non-parties as well as parties. Paragraphs 60 and 61 require a PSC programme consistent with the relevant Assembly resolution, carried out only by authorized and qualified port State control officers; paragraph 62 requires those officers to be free from commercial, financial and other pressures, to hold no commercial interest in the port, the ships inspected, repair facilities or support services, and not to be employed by or work on behalf of recognized organizations or classification societies.

Both parts close as Part 2 does: paragraphs 51 and 63 require the coastal State and the port State to periodically evaluate their own performance in exercising their rights and meeting their obligations. That symmetry - implement, enforce, evaluate - is the single most useful thing to carry into the exam hall, because it lets you structure all three States from one remembered shape.

The printed marks are 6 + 4 + 6 and the question hides four tasks inside limb (a): objective, strategy, instruments, and the implied "what is this Code". Splitting (a) across route steps 2, 3 and 4 stops the six marks being spent on a single paragraph about the objective. Limb (b) is only four marks but has a precise source - paragraphs 43 and 44 - so a candidate who names the indicators verbatim banks those marks quickly and buys time for limb (c).

Limb (c) covers three States in six marks. Two marks each. The Code makes that easy because Parts 2, 3 and 4 share a skeleton: implementation, enforcement, evaluation and review. Answer all three on that skeleton and the examiner sees structure rather than a list.

blocks.h: The mandatory-application chain, and why it matters

blocks.p: Candidates often assert that "the III Code is mandatory" without being able to say why a recommendatory-sounding text binds anybody. The answer is that the Code itself was never redrafted into obligation language; instead the conventions were amended to require its use. That is why the Code still reads "should" throughout. Being able to say this in one sentence distinguishes a candidate who has read the instrument from one who has read about it.

The audit scheme is the practical consequence. The Code supplies the auditable areas; A.1187(33) supplies the obligation-by-obligation list that auditors and Administrations work from. A.1187(33) was adopted 6 December 2023, replacing the 2021 list, A.1157(32) - three months before this sitting. Material citing the 2021 list is superseded.

The printed words are "Which all IMO instruments covered in the code". Two things are being asked at once and the safe answer gives both. The Code's scope at paragraph 6 is expressed as six subject areas, not as a list of conventions. The instruments under which the Code is mandatory are the SOLAS / MARPOL / STCW / Load Lines / Tonnage / COLREG family with their Protocols, listed in A.1187(33).

A count is risky. The audit scope is usually summarised as nine mandatory instruments - SOLAS 1974, SOLAS PROT 1988, MARPOL, MARPOL PROT 1997, STCW 1978, LL 1966, LL PROT 1988, TONNAGE 1969 and COLREG 1972 - but A.1187(33) annex 1 also carries a SOLAS PROT 1978 column, and neither the Code nor A.1187(33) states a number anywhere. List them; do not lead with a count. If a count is wanted, say "the SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG instruments together with their Protocols, commonly summarised as nine".

The absence of maritime security from paragraph 6 is a genuine examinable point, not a drafting slip: the preamble uses the phrase "safety, security and protection of the marine environment" while the operative scope does not extend to security instruments.

ul: Writing a general essay on flag State duties under UNCLOS article 94. That is a different question. The examiner has named a specific Code and wants its paragraphs.
Answering limb (a)'s "which instruments" with the six subject areas only, or with the convention list only. Give both and say why they differ.
Confusing the III Code with the ISM Code. The III Code binds States; the ISM Code binds companies and ships.
Treating the performance indicators as something the flag State reports to IMO. They are for the State's own periodic self-evaluation under paragraph 42.
Giving the coastal State a control-and-inspection role. Paragraph 48 is a list of services - SAR, hydrography, VTS, aids to navigation.
Spending half the answer on limb (c) because it is familiar. It is worth six marks, the same as limb (a).
Six subject areas versus the instrument list. The single most likely place to lose marks on this question.
"Should" throughout the Code. If asked whether the Code is mandatory, the answer is that its use is mandatory under the amended conventions, while the text remains recommendatory in form.
Excluding constructive total losses. Paragraph 43 says annual loss statistics excluding CTLs. Reproducing that qualifier shows the source has been read.

Independence. Two independence requirements appear, in different Parts and for different reasons - the flag State's audit programme must be independent of the certifying body (16.2), and PSCOs must be free of commercial interest and not work for recognized organizations (62). Do not merge them.
A.1054(27) was revoked. An answer that cites the 2011 Code as current is citing a revoked instrument.
"Is the III Code mandatory, and how?" - use the amendment chain.
"What is IMSAS and what does it audit against?" - the Code supplies the auditable areas; A.1187(33) supplies the obligations list.

"Your flag State has a rising detention rate. What does the Code expect it to do?" - paragraphs 43 and 44: treat it as a performance indicator, review detentions against fleet size, review responses to PSC deficiency reports, and test whether staffing and resources are adequate.

"What must a flag State do before authorising a class society?" - paragraph 18: capability, a formal written agreement, specific instructions for unfit ships, national law and interpretations, records.
"Name three port State obligations under the Code." - reception facilities, port State control, register of fuel oil suppliers.

"Which State investigates a casualty, and who gets the report?" - paragraphs 38 and 41: the flag State provides qualified investigators irrespective of casualty location; the report goes to the Organization with the flag State's observations.

blocks.p: Two shapes carry the whole question. The Code's shape is common areas, then flag, then coastal, then port. The shape inside each State part is implementation, enforcement, evaluation and review. Everything in limb (c) hangs on the second shape, and limb (b) is simply the "evaluation and review" box of the flag State part opened up.

For the coastal State's eight services, group them as talk, warn, rescue, chart (radiocommunication, meteorological warnings, SAR, hydrographic) and route, report, watch, mark (ships' routeing, ship reporting, VTS, aids to navigation).

blocks.h: Flag State surveyors and investigations - the detail behind route step 6

blocks.p: Limb (c) is six marks for three States, so the Model Answer gives the flag State the headline of paragraphs 28 to 41 rather than the whole regime. The detail below is worth holding for the oral, and for any future question that asks about surveyor competence directly.

ul: Qualification (para 29). Either appropriate qualifications from a marine or nautical institution with relevant seagoing experience as a certificated officer holding or having held a valid management level certificate of competency, with maintained technical knowledge; or a degree or equivalent from a tertiary institution in a relevant field of engineering or science recognised by the flag State; or accreditation as a surveyor through a formalised training programme reaching the same standard.

Experience (paras 30-31). Personnel qualified under 29.1 should have served not less than three years at sea as a deck or engine officer; those qualified under 29.2 should have worked in a relevant capacity for at least three years.

Knowledge (para 36). The qualification should encompass knowledge of the applicable international and national rules; of survey, certification, control, investigative and oversight procedures; understanding of the goals of the instruments and of the processes both on board and ashore; professional competency; full safety awareness; and training or experience in the tasks performed.
Identification (para 37). The flag State issues an identification document for the surveyor to carry when performing his or her tasks.

Investigator expertise (para 39). Ready access is required to expertise in navigation and the Collision Regulations, flag State certificate-of-competency regulations, causes of marine pollution, interviewing techniques, evidence gathering, and evaluation of the effects of the human element.

Reporting threshold (para 40). Any accident involving personal injury necessitating absence from duty of three days or more, and any deaths resulting from occupational accidents and casualties, should be investigated and the results made public.

blocks.p: The answer deliberately does not lead with a number of instruments. A.1070(28) states six subject areas and states no instrument count; A.1187(33) lists obligations by instrument without totalling them. The figure of nine is a widely used summary of the mandatory instruments and is offered as such, not as a quotation from either resolution. A candidate who writes "nine" will not be marked wrong, but a candidate who lists the instruments cannot be.

The Framework and Procedures for the Member State Audit Scheme was not re-read for this answer, so no claim is made here about audit periodicity or about the scheme's own procedural rules. The answer restricts itself to what the Code and the obligations list say.

questions.understand_first: The examiner has named one instrument and is checking whether you have opened it. Every mark on this question is inside resolution A.1070(28). The Code is short - sixty-three paragraphs in four parts - and it is organised exactly the way the question is: common material first, then flag, coastal and port States in that order, each ending with an evaluation and review section. Limb (b) is that evaluation section of the flag State part. So if you can hold the Code's own structure, you can rebuild the whole answer from it. The one place the question is sharper than the Code is "which all IMO instruments" - because the Code answers that with six SUBJECT AREAS, while the instruments it is mandatory under are a different list entirely.
questions.memory_cue: The Code's four parts give the answer its spine: COMMON, FLAG, COASTAL, PORT. Walk it as WHAT-WHY-HOW-WHICH-MEASURE-WHO: WHAT the Code is (1), WHY it exists - the objective (2), HOW a State meets it - the strategy (3), WHICH instruments it reaches (4), how performance is MEASURED (5), and WHO does what - flag (6), then coastal and port (7).

quick_revision.recall_15s: III Code = annex to A.1070(28), 4 December 2013; revoked A.1054(27). Recommendatory in wording, mandatory in use because SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, LL, TONNAGE and COLREG were amended to require it. Objective (para 1): enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment and assist States in implementing IMO instruments. Strategy (para 3): develop an overall strategy, establish a methodology to monitor and assess it, continuously review it. Scope (para 6): six subject areas - safety of life at sea, prevention of pollution, STCW, load lines, tonnage, COLREG; security is not one. KPIs (paras 42-44): PSC detention rates, flag State inspection results, casualty statistics, communication and information processes, annual loss statistics excluding CTLs, plus ten review areas. Parts 2, 3 and 4 all run implementation - enforcement - evaluation and review.

quick_revision.critical_regulation: A.1070(28) annex paragraph 6 - the Code addresses six subject areas: safety of life at sea; prevention of pollution from ships; standards of training, certification and watchkeeping; load lines; tonnage measurement; and regulations for preventing collisions at sea. Read it with paragraphs 42 to 44, which carry the flag State performance indicators.
quick_revision.major_trap: Answering "which IMO instruments" with only one of the two correct lists. Paragraph 6 gives six SUBJECT AREAS and does not name conventions; the treaty instruments under which the Code is mandatory are SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG with their Protocols, listed in A.1187(33). Maritime security is in neither the paragraph 6 list nor the Code's operative scope.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Give the route for the III Code question.
retrieval_cards.answer: 1 The Code and what made it mandatory. 2 (a) The objective. 3 (a) The strategy. 4 (a) Which instruments. 5 (b) The performance indicators. 6 (c) Flag State. 7 (c) Coastal and port State.
retrieval_cards.why: Steps 2, 3 and 4 split limb (a), which hides three separate tasks in six marks.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which resolution contains the III Code, when was it adopted, and what did it revoke?
retrieval_cards.answer: Resolution A.1070(28), adopted 4 December 2013. Operative paragraph 3 revoked A.1054(27), the Code for the Implementation of Mandatory IMO Instruments, 2011.
retrieval_cards.why: Citing the revoked 2011 Code as current is a common and visible error.

retrieval_cards.prompt: State the objective of the III Code in the Code's own words.
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 1: to enhance global maritime safety and protection of the marine environment, and to assist States in the implementation of instruments of the Organization.
retrieval_cards.why: The second half - assistance - is routinely dropped, and it is half the sentence.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What three things does paragraph 3 recommend a State do to meet the objective?
retrieval_cards.answer: Develop an overall strategy covering its flag, port and coastal responsibilities; establish a methodology to monitor and assess that the strategy delivers effective implementation and enforcement; and continuously review the strategy to achieve, maintain and improve organizational performance and capability.
retrieval_cards.why: This is the "strategy recommended to flag state" half of limb (a).

retrieval_cards.prompt: The question asks which IMO instruments the Code covers. Why are there two answers?
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 6 defines the Code's scope as six SUBJECT AREAS - safety of life at sea, prevention of pollution from ships, STCW, load lines, tonnage measurement, COLREG. Separately, the Code is made mandatory by amendments to the treaty INSTRUMENTS - SOLAS, MARPOL, STCW and its Code, Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG with their Protocols, listed in A.1187(33). Give both.
retrieval_cards.why: The highest-value distinction on this question.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Which subject area is conspicuously absent from paragraph 6?
retrieval_cards.answer: Maritime security. The preamble speaks of safety, security and environmental protection, but the six subject areas in the operative scope do not include security, so the ISPS Code and SOLAS chapter XI-2 sit outside the Code's stated scope.
retrieval_cards.why: A candidate who lists seven areas including security has not read paragraph 6.

retrieval_cards.prompt: List the flag State performance indicators at paragraph 43.
retrieval_cards.answer: Port State control detention rates; flag State inspection results; casualty statistics; communication and information processes; annual loss statistics excluding constructive total losses; and other appropriate indicators. Their purpose is to determine whether staffing, resources and administrative procedures are adequate.
retrieval_cards.why: Limb (b) is four marks and this paragraph is the whole of it.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Two independence requirements appear in the Code. What are they and where?
retrieval_cards.answer: Paragraph 16.2 - the flag State's audit and inspection programme must be independent of any body issuing the certificates, including a delegated entity. Paragraph 62 - port State control officers must be free of commercial, financial and other pressure, hold no commercial interest in the port or ships inspected, and not be employed by or work for recognized organizations or classification societies.
retrieval_cards.why: They serve different purposes in different Parts and are often merged into one.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the eight coastal State areas at paragraph 48.
retrieval_cards.answer: Radiocommunication services; meteorological services and warnings; search and rescue services; hydrographic services; ships' routeing; ship reporting systems; vessel traffic services; and aids to navigation.
retrieval_cards.why: They are services to shipping, not controls over ships - which is the point of Part 3.

retrieval_cards.prompt: Name the three port State obligations at paragraph 56.
retrieval_cards.answer: Provision of appropriate reception facilities, or the capability to accept all waste streams regulated under IMO instruments; port State control; and keeping a register of fuel oil suppliers.
retrieval_cards.why: The register of fuel oil suppliers is the one candidates forget.

retrieval_cards.prompt: The Code says "should" throughout. How is it mandatory?
retrieval_cards.answer: The Code was not redrafted into obligation language. Its USE was made mandatory by amendments to the conventions - A.1083(28), A.1084(28) and A.1085(28) for Load Lines, Tonnage and COLREG; MSC.366(93), MSC.373(93), MSC.374(93) and MSC.375(93) for SOLAS, STCW, the STCW Code and the 1988 Load Lines Protocol; MEPC.246(66) and MEPC.247(66) for MARPOL and its 1997 Protocol.
retrieval_cards.why: Explains the mismatch between the Code's wording and its legal effect.

retrieval_cards.prompt: What single shape do Parts 2, 3 and 4 of the Code share?
retrieval_cards.answer: Implementation, then enforcement, then evaluation and review. Each of the flag, coastal and port State parts is built on it, and paragraphs 42, 51 and 63 are the three evaluation requirements.
retrieval_cards.why: One remembered shape answers limb (c) for all three States and locates limb (b).

decomposition_gate.question_intent: Three limbs against one named Code. Limb (a) is really three tasks - objective, strategy, instruments - for six marks. Limb (b) is a precise recall of one section of the Code for four marks. Limb (c) asks for all three State roles in six marks, which the Code makes tractable because Parts 2, 3 and 4 share a structure.

decomposition_gate.examiner_expectation: That the candidate has opened A.1070(28). The tell-tales are the paragraph 3 strategy in its three parts, the six subject areas at paragraph 6, the CTL exclusion at paragraph 43, the eight coastal services at 48 and the three port obligations at 56. General UNCLOS flag-State material scores poorly because it is not what was asked.
primary_source_plan: Obtain A.1070(28) in full rather than a summary - the paragraph numbers are the marks
Map objective, strategy and scope to paragraphs 1, 3 and 6 before drafting

Read A.1187(33) for the instrument list and the mandatory-application chain
Do not assert an instrument count that neither resolution states

decomposition_gate.jurisdiction_risk: LOW. The Code applies to States generally and India is a Party to the instruments concerned. No Indian statute is load-bearing on this answer.

How many treaty instruments the audit scope contains - not stated in either resolution

Whether maritime security falls within the Code's scope - it does not, at paragraph 6
Whether the performance indicators are reported externally or used internally
